540.title: Hidden from the wise (Luke 10:21–24)
540.hook: Jesus rejoices that simple people understand
540.howItsDone: Many Christians treasure Luke 10:21 as a reminder that faith is open to everyone, and teachers of prayer across traditions often speak of receiving God like a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seventy sent out two by two. Your line was peace be to this house. Did you carry peace through a door? Day five hundred forty.

The Gospels show Jesus weeping, sighing, angry at injustice, tired enough to sleep through a storm. They seldom say outright that he was joyful. That's what makes today's four verses stand out. The seventy have just come back, buzzing with stories, and Jesus has told them: rejoice that your names are written in heaven. And then Luke says: "In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit." The Greek verb is stronger than the English. It's the word for exulting, being overjoyed, the same family of words Mary used when she sang that her spirit rejoiced in God. What could make him that happy? Not who you'd expect.

Here's what he says, in the King James words: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight." Babes, in Greek nepioi, means little children, infants. Not the experts. Not the people with the best schooling or the highest positions. Luke never tells us who the seventy were, only that they were sent out with no purse and no bag, and they've just seen what many learned people missed. Jesus isn't against learning. Luke himself opens his Gospel saying he investigated everything carefully. The point is about the door you come in by. Some things you don't grasp by being clever. You grasp them the way a child does: by trusting, by receiving, by not pretending you already know. The wise and prudent, the people who are sure they understand, can find the door closed precisely because they're sure. Then Jesus turns to his disciples privately: "Blessed are the eyes which see the things that ye see: For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them." Kings. Prophets. Isaiah, David, all the great names. They longed to see this, and the ones who got to see it are a group of ordinary people from Galilee. It's a strange, warm reversal, and it fits Luke's whole Gospel: the shepherds before the priests, the widow before the rich, the child set beside him. The ones who receive are the ones who know they need to.
screen: then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE EYES WHICH SEE THE THINGS THAT YE SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone the world wouldn't call an expert. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who've taught you the most important things, not from a stage, but by how they lived. A grandmother who prayed while she cooked. A child who forgave quickly. A coworker with no title who always knew the right thing to do. Someone with a disability, or a hard life, who sees what others miss. Let one face come. What did they understand that cleverness couldn't teach? Then think of someone you'll meet today whom you might overlook as a teacher. Decide to listen to them as if they knew something you don't. If you pray, you can give thanks for your unexpected teachers. If you don't, simply honor them. The bell holds the time.
Nepioi, Greek for little children, infants: Jesus rejoices that what the clever missed has been revealed to little children, ordinary people who simply received it.
Your line: revealed to babes. Today, ask one person you'd normally overlook what they think, and really listen to the answer. Day five hundred forty.

541.title: Who is my neighbor? (Luke 10:25–37)
541.hook: a lawyer's question and a story that asks who acted like a neighbor
541.howItsDone: Hospitals, charities and the emergency-helper laws known as Good Samaritan laws take their name from this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus rejoicing that things hidden from the wise were revealed to babes. Your line was revealed to babes. Who did you listen to that you might have overlooked? Day five hundred forty-one.

It starts as a test. A lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, stands up and asks: "Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus turns it back: what does the law say? How do you read it? And the lawyer answers well, joining two lines from his own scriptures, from Deuteronomy and Leviticus: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind; and thy neighbour as thyself." Jesus says: right. "This do, and thou shalt live." But the lawyer, Luke says, wanting to justify himself, asks one more question. A question about where the edges are.

"And who is my neighbour?" Who counts? Where can I stop? Jesus answers with a story. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead." A priest comes along and passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, does the same. The text doesn't tell us why. Readers have offered guesses, fear, hurry, worry about touching what might be a corpse, but Luke is silent. Then a Samaritan comes: one of the same people whose village, a chapter ago, would not receive Jesus. "And when he saw him, he had compassion on him." The same words Luke used for Jesus at the widow's gate in Nain. He bandages the wounds, pouring in oil and wine. He puts the man on his own animal and walks. He leaves two coins with the innkeeper, two pence in the King James, and says: "Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee." Then Jesus flips the lawyer's question. Not who is my neighbor, but this: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" Notice that the lawyer doesn't say the word Samaritan; some readers think he couldn't bring himself to. He says: "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus: "Go, and do thou likewise." The lawyer wanted a boundary. He gets a verb. Neighbor isn't a category of people you owe. It's something you become.
screen: `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR? WHERE DO I STOP?`
`A PRIEST, A LEVITE: THE OTHER SIDE.`
`NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO WAS A NEIGHBOR.`
then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a neighbor to someone unexpected. Settle, and breathe. Think about your own road: the commute, the street, the hallway at work, the group chat. Who's lying by the side of it? Not literally, maybe. Someone who's been left out, knocked down by bad news, stuck. And now the harder part: think of someone you wouldn't expect to help, or wouldn't expect to help you. Someone from the other side of some line, politics, faith, class, a family feud. Hold them in mind without arguing. Picture crossing the road toward them, the way the Samaritan did. What would one small act of mercy look like? If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply picture the crossing. The bell holds the time.
Plesion, the Greek word behind neighbor, meaning the one near you: a lawyer's question, and Jesus' story of a Samaritan who stops on the road, turning the question into who acted as a neighbor.
Your line: go and do likewise. Cross one road today toward someone you'd usually pass by, and do one small, practical thing. Day five hundred forty-one.

542.title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
542.hook: Martha is busy and cross; Mary sits at his feet; one thing is needed
542.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a short time of quiet prayer or Bible reading before the day's work begins, and in monastic communities, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican, the day is shaped by set hours of prayer between hours of work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lawyer asked who is my neighbor, and a Samaritan answered with oil, wine and his own animal. Your line was go and do likewise. Who turned out to be your neighbor? Day five hundred forty-two.

Luke tells this story in five verses, and he puts it straight after the good Samaritan. That placement matters. Yesterday's hero was the man who stopped and did something. Today, a guest arrives at a house in a village, and the person doing everything gets a gentle word. Luke says a woman named Martha received him into her house. Her house, her welcome, her guest. Luke only says there was much serving; it isn't hard to imagine bread to bake and water to carry. And her sister Mary is sitting on the floor, listening. Anyone who has been the one at the sink while others laugh in the next room may recognize Martha.
screen: `ONE AT THE SINK, ONE ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." That phrase is bigger than it sounds. Sitting at a teacher's feet was the place of a student; Paul later says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Mary takes that place, one some readers think was usually kept for men, and nobody sends her back to the kitchen. Martha, meanwhile, "was cumbered about much serving." Luke's Greek word has the sense of being pulled around, drawn in every direction. Finally she comes in and says: "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me." Notice she doesn't speak to Mary. She goes over her head. And the answer is gentle. He says her name twice, the way you do with someone you love: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her." Careful here means full of care, anxious. He doesn't tell Martha to stop cooking. He doesn't call serving wrong; one story earlier, the Samaritan was all service. What he names is the worry, the many things crowding out the one. Christians have read the sisters in more than one way. Some early writers saw two callings, the active life and the quiet life of prayer, and monasteries tried to keep both. Others say every person has a Martha and a Mary inside. And Martha gets her own great moment later: in John's Gospel, she is the one who tells Jesus plainly that she believes he is the Christ. Nobody here is the villain. One sister just needed to sit down first.

Here's the practice: sit before you serve. Before the next thing on your list, stop and sit down, the way Mary did, as if someone worth listening to were in the room. Let the list wait. Notice the many things pulling at you. Name two or three of them, and set each one down for these two minutes. If you pray, you can simply listen, without asking for anything. If you don't, listen to the quiet, to your breath, to whatever is actually here. When the bell rings, get up and serve, but from having sat first. The bell holds the time.
Martha. The sister who welcomed Jesus into her home and was pulled in every direction by much serving, while Mary sat at his feet and listened.
Your line: one thing is needful. Today, when you feel dragged in every direction, stop for a breath and ask what the one thing is, right now. Day five hundred forty-two.

543.title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–4)
543.hook: Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer
543.howItsDone: Christians say the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home, usually in Matthew's wording; some churches add the closing doxology straight after it, while the Catholic Mass places it after a short prayer by the priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha in the kitchen and Mary at his feet. Your line was one thing is needful. Did you manage to sit before you served? Day five hundred forty-three.

Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer: at his baptism, all night before choosing the twelve, on the mountain when his face changed. Today it happens again. He is praying in a certain place, and his friends wait nearby until he finishes. They stand a little way off and watch. When he stops, one of them asks a question. Not about miracles, not about the kingdom, not about who's the greatest. Just this: show us how.

In the King James Bible, the disciple says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John the Baptist had taught his followers to pray, Luke says. Now they want to be taught too. And what Jesus gives is short. The King James text of Luke reads much like Matthew's; some modern Bibles print Luke's version shorter still, opening with one word, Father, and then five requests. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Bread for each day. Forgiveness. And protection from the time of trial. That's it. Two small differences from Matthew are worth hearing. Luke's bread line in the King James is "Give us day by day our daily bread." Day by day: not a stockpile, a habit. And where Matthew says debts, Luke says: "And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us." Sins for what we've done, debts for what others owe us. Matthew uses debts for both. One more surprise: the closing line, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, isn't in Luke at all, even in the King James. The King James has it in Matthew. Some churches say it straight after the prayer; in the Catholic Mass it comes a moment later, after another short prayer by the priest. So a prayer said in churches today began as a short answer to a simple request. Teach us.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray Luke's version, slowly. Settle and breathe. If you pray, you can say the King James lines one per breath, leaving long gaps: Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Give us day by day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation. If you don't pray, take just one of those five requests and sit with it. Which one names something you actually need today? Bread, forgiveness, protection? Let it stay with you until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Father. The one word Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer opens with, a disciple's request after watching Jesus pray, answered with just five requests after it.
Your line: teach us. Today, ask someone to show you one thing they do well, and listen like a student. Day five hundred forty-three.

544.title: A friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–13)
544.hook: a friend knocks for bread at midnight and keeps knocking
544.howItsDone: Some Christians bring the same request to God again and again, in personal prayer, in prayer lists kept by churches, and in intercessions during Sunday worship, reading this story as permission to keep asking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disciple watched Jesus pray and said, show us how, the prayer beginning with the word Father. Your line was teach us. Who did you ask to teach you something? Day five hundred forty-four.

Straight after giving the prayer, Jesus tells a story with a very practical problem in it. It's midnight. A friend has turned up from a journey, tired and hungry, and there is nothing in the house to set before him. Not a loaf. Nobody wants to be the host with an empty table and a guest at the door. There is one option left. Walk down the dark lane to a neighbor's house, where the door is shut and the children are already in bed, and knock. Loudly enough to be heard.

In the King James Bible, the man at the door calls out: "Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him?" And from inside comes an answer any parent of small children might give: "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee." Getting up means opening the door and waking the children. But the knocking doesn't stop. Jesus says the neighbor will get up, not because they're friends, but "because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity is the old English word. The Greek is anaideia, and it means shamelessness, a nerve that doesn't care how it looks. Readers differ about whose shamelessness it is. Some hear the knocker's, refusing to give up. Others hear the sleeper's, getting up to avoid the shame of failing a neighbor. Either way, here's the turn. The story isn't saying God is a grumpy neighbor who has to be nagged. It works by contrast: if even a sleepy friend gets up at midnight, how much more will God. Then come the words: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." And Luke ends with a twist of his own. Matthew says the Father gives good things. Luke says: "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" Luke's last word here is not bread at all, but the Holy Spirit.
screen: `TROUBLE ME NOT: THE DOOR IS SHUT.`
`NOT A GRUMPY GOD: HOW MUCH MORE.`
then, large: `KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask boldly, like a friend at a friend's door. Settle and breathe. Think of one thing you need, really need, that you've stopped asking for because it felt embarrassing, or greedy, or too late. Let it come to mind plainly. If you pray, you can ask for it in your own words, the way you'd ask a friend, without polishing the request. Then ask again. If you don't pray, simply let yourself admit the need without apologizing for it. Notice what it's like to name it plainly. The bell holds the time.

Anaideia, Greek for shamelessness, nerve, which the King James Bible calls importunity: a man knocks on a barred door at midnight for three loaves and keeps knocking, and the story says, how much more will God give.
Your line: shamelessly ask. Today, ask one person for help you've been too proud to request, and don't apologize for asking. Day five hundred forty-four.

545.title: The lamp of the eye (Luke 11:14–36)
545.hook: take heed that the light in you is not darkness
545.howItsDone: Some Christians practice a slow, attentive looking as prayer, with icons in Orthodox churches, with art and nature in many retreat traditions, and with the Ignatian habit of noticing where God was present in the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a friend at midnight kept knocking on a barred door for three loaves. Your line was shamelessly ask. Did you ask for the help you needed? Day five hundred forty-five.

This part of Luke is noisy. Jesus heals a man who couldn't speak, and some in the crowd say he does it by the power of the prince of demons. He answers that a house divided against itself falls. A woman shouts a blessing on his mother. Others demand a sign from heaven before they'll believe anything. Accusations, arguments, people shouting from the back. And in the middle of all that heat, he stops and talks about something quiet: a lamp in a room, and the light that comes in through your eyes.

First, the lamp. Nobody lights one and hides it under a bushel; you set it on a stand so whoever walks in can see. Then, in the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness." Single sounds odd to us. The Greek word, haplous, means simple, whole, undivided: an eye that sees clearly because it isn't split between ten things. And here's a detail that changes how it sounds. In Jesus' world, a good eye and an evil eye were also ways of talking about money and people. A generous person had a good eye; a stingy, envious one had an evil eye. Proverbs says it this way: "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor." Paul later uses a word from the same family as haplous for generosity. So the saying is about more than eyesight. How you look at people fills you up. Look at the world with envy or suspicion, and the darkness gets inside. Look with a clear, generous eye, and you fill with light. Then the warning, short and sharp: "Take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness." It's possible to think you're seeing clearly and be wrong. In a chapter full of people who looked straight at a healing and saw the devil, that line lands hard. The crowd wanted a sign from the sky. He points them back to their own eyes.
screen: `A GOOD EYE IS A GENEROUS EYE.`
then, large: `THE LIGHT OF THE BODY IS THE EYE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something beautiful. Find one thing in front of you, or out of a window: a tree, a face in a photo, the light on a wall, a cup. Let your eyes rest on it, and only on it. When your attention splits, bring it back. Look at it generously, the way you'd look at something you love, without judging it or wanting anything from it. Notice what happens inside you as you look. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you see. The bell holds the time.
Haplous, Greek for single, simple, whole: Jesus says the eye is the body's light, and a clear, generous eye like that fills you with light, while an envious one lets the darkness in.
Your line: keep the light in. Today, when you catch yourself looking at someone with envy or suspicion, look again, on purpose, with a generous eye. Day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: Clean on the outside (Luke 11:37–54)
546.hook: he eats with Pharisees and challenges religion that's all surface
546.howItsDone: Some Christians pair outward practices, like grace before meals, tithing or fasting, with an inward examination of conscience, and the season of Lent joins fasting with prayer and almsgiving, the giving this passage names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lamp of the eye, and a single, generous eye that fills the whole body with light. Your line was keep the light in. Did you look at someone again, on purpose? Day five hundred forty-six.

A Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner. That alone is worth noticing: Luke shows him at Pharisees' tables more than once. And the Pharisees in this scene care about holiness at the table itself: washing, tithing, cups and dishes. So when the guest sits straight down without washing, the host is startled. The King James Bible says he "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner." And Jesus, at someone else's table, answers the look on his face.

"Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness." Ravening means grabbing, greed. It's a sharp thing to say at dinner, and Luke doesn't soften it. Then a question that turns it into a riddle: "did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also?" God made the cup's inside as well as its outside. You can't polish one and ignore the other. His answer to how is surprising: give alms from what's within, and everything is clean. Generosity cleans the inside of the cup. Then he names their careful tithing, a tenth of even mint and rue from the herb garden, and says they pass over justice and the love of God. But listen to how the sentence ends: "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." He doesn't throw out the small faithful habits. He says do both. This is the language of Israel's own prophets, speaking to their own people. Micah asked what the Lord requires, and answered: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. It's an argument inside a family, and any church can hear it about itself. And so a week on the road closes. Wisdom given to little ones. A Samaritan who stopped. Martha and Mary. A short prayer. A friend knocking at midnight. A lamp in the eye. And now a cup that needs washing on both sides.
screen: `DO BOTH: THE SMALL AND THE GREAT.`
then, large: `NOT TO LEAVE THE OTHER UNDONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean something inside, not just outside. If there's a cup or a bowl near you, pick it up and look into it. If not, picture one. Then turn your attention inward. What's sitting inside you that nobody else can see? A grudge, a little greed, a story you tell yourself about someone. Don't scrub at it. Just name it honestly. Then think of one generous thing you could give today, from the inside out: time, money, a kind word you've been holding back. If you pray, you can offer that inside place to God as it is. If you don't, simply let it be named. The bell holds the time.
Alms. Jesus's answer to how the inside of the cup gets clean: give from what's within to the poor, and everything is made clean.
Your line: the inside too. Today, when you tidy up to be seen by someone, do one quiet, generous thing nobody will see. Day five hundred forty-six, and another week on the path.

fork.setup: you're the host. your honored guest sits down to eat without the ritual washing. what happens next in the story?
options: you ask him to leave.
you say nothing, but you're startled, and he answers your look.
you wash his hands for him.
fork.reveal: the Pharisee "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner," and Jesus answers with the cup: the inside matters too.

original.note: Greek: from within, the inside. the part of the cup, and of a person, that Jesus says God also made.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was against religious rules.
what it means: he says the outward habits should be done, and the inside cleaned too, through justice, love of God and generosity.
what a scholar hears: he speaks as Israel's prophets did, from inside the tradition, as a guest at a Pharisee's table, not from outside it.
